column2: Define date boundaries with {{c1::CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION}} PF_OrderDate(DATETIME2) AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES ('20240101', '20240401');
column3:
The dates define three key ranges. With RANGE RIGHT, April 1 belongs to the range starting on April 1 rather than the one before it.
Review source

column2: Map PF_OrderDate to storage with {{c1::CREATE PARTITION SCHEME}} PS_OrderDate AS PARTITION PF_OrderDate ALL TO ([PRIMARY]);
column3:
The function defines the ranges first. This statement maps the resulting partitions to storage without changing where the boundaries fall.
Review source

column2: In a partition scheme, {{c1::ALL TO ([PRIMARY])}} maps every partition to the PRIMARY filegroup.
column3:
The clause places every range on PRIMARY, but the table remains partitioned. Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Fabric use only PRIMARY for this purpose.
Review source

column2: Place a table on PS_OrderDate using OrderDate as its partitioning column with the final clause {{c1::ON PS_OrderDate(OrderDate)}}.
column3:
The scheme determines storage and OrderDate supplies each row's key value. The function associated with the scheme assigns that value to a partition.
Review source

column2: A partition function with four distinct boundary values creates {{c1::five partitions}}.
column3:
Each boundary divides a range into two. With four cuts there is a range before the first boundary, three between boundaries, and one after the last.
Review source

column2: For RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES (100, 200), the value 100 maps to partition {{c1::2}}.
column3:
The first range ends just below 100. RANGE RIGHT places the boundary value itself at the start of the second range.
Review source

column2: For RANGE LEFT FOR VALUES (100, 200), the value 100 maps to partition {{c1::1}}.
column3:
The first range ends at 100 and includes it. Only values greater than 100 move into the next range.
Review source

column2: If neither LEFT nor RIGHT is specified in a partition function, SQL Server uses {{c1::RANGE LEFT}}.
column3:
LEFT includes a boundary in the range immediately before it. Specify the direction when a date at exactly midnight must fall in a particular range.
Review source

column2: With RANGE RIGHT and final DATETIME2 boundary '20241001', the partition beginning October 1 has {{c1::no later explicit boundary}}.
column3:
The last range stretches from October 1 to the end of the data type's valid values. Add another boundary to isolate just those three months.
Review source

column2: For a clustered primary key partitioned on PS_OrderDate(OrderDate), use PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, {{c1::OrderDate}}).
column3:
OrderDate is required in the key because the unique index uses it to partition rows. The resulting constraint allows the same OrderID on different dates.
Review source

column2: PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, OrderDate) enforces uniqueness of {{c1::the column pair}}, not OrderID alone.
column3:
Two rows can share an OrderID if their OrderDate values differ. Enforcing OrderID alone requires a separate uniqueness design.
Review source

column2: Given dbo.Orders uses PS_OrderDate(OrderDate), align its index with CREATE INDEX IX_Customer ON dbo.Orders(CustomerID) {{c1::ON PS_OrderDate(OrderDate)}};
column3:
The ON clause sends index entries to the same ranges as the table. SQL Server can add OrderDate as a nonkey included column in this nonunique index.
Review source

column2: Given partition function PF_OrderDate, locate a date with SELECT {{c1::$PARTITION}}.PF_OrderDate('20240515');
column3:
The function tells you where the date belongs even if no row has that date. Its return value reflects the current boundary definitions.
Review source

column2: Count rows per nonempty partition with SELECT $PARTITION.PF_OrderDate(OrderDate), COUNT(*) FROM dbo.Orders {{c1::GROUP BY $PARTITION.PF_OrderDate(OrderDate)}};
column3:
COUNT(*) summarizes the rows that actually exist in each range. A partition with no rows contributes no group to the result.
Review source

column2: Given a new boundary and schemes ready for a split, use ALTER PARTITION FUNCTION PF_OrderDate() {{c1::SPLIT RANGE}} ('20250101');
column3:
SPLIT RANGE inserts a boundary that is not already present. The existing range becomes two, and associated schemes must have a destination ready.
Review source

column2: For PF_OrderDate with existing boundary '20240401', remove it with ALTER PARTITION FUNCTION PF_OrderDate() {{c1::MERGE RANGE}} ('20240401');
column3:
MERGE RANGE removes that existing boundary. Rows from the two adjacent ranges are still stored after the change.
Review source

column2: Prepare PS_OrderDate to receive another partition on PRIMARY with ALTER PARTITION SCHEME PS_OrderDate {{c1::NEXT USED [PRIMARY]}};
column3:
NEXT USED chooses where the next new partition will go. Review the designation again before a later split.
Review source

column2: Before SPLIT RANGE, every partition scheme using the function must have a {{c1::NEXT USED filegroup}}.
column3:
Every dependent scheme needs a destination even if some of them point to the same filegroup. A single missing designation can block the whole operation.
Review source

column2: Assuming SWITCH requirements are met, archive partition 2 with ALTER TABLE dbo.Orders {{c1::SWITCH}} PARTITION 2 TO dbo.OrdersArchive;
column3:
This reassigns the second partition's pages to the archive table. It does not copy rows or move pages to a different filegroup.
Review source

column2: Rebuild only partition 3 of a partitioned IX_Customer index with ALTER INDEX IX_Customer ON dbo.Orders REBUILD {{c1::PARTITION = 3}};
column3:
The partition number limits this rebuild to one part of IX_Customer. The rest of the index does not get rebuilt by this statement.
Review source

column2: Create per-partition statistics on an eligible partitioned table with CREATE STATISTICS ST_OrderDate ON dbo.Orders(OrderDate) WITH {{c1::INCREMENTAL = ON}};
column3:
Incremental statistics maintain partition-level information that SQL Server can combine. That lets it update statistics for a changed partition without always scanning all partitions.
Review source

column2: Choose daily, monthly, or yearly partition intervals according to {{c1::data volume and retention needs}}.
column3:
A useful interval groups enough rows for efficient maintenance and matches how old data is retired. Daily ranges are not automatically better than monthly ones.
Review source

column2: With an enabled columnstore index on a table, SPLIT RANGE requires the partition being split to be {{c1::empty}}.
column3:
The columnstore restriction means you cannot split a populated range while the index is enabled. Create empty future ranges before loading their rows.
Review source

column2: Two partition functions with different names can still align an index and its table if their definitions are {{c1::equivalent}}.
column3:
Matching range definitions means the same row maps to the same numbered partition. Function names themselves do not determine alignment.
Review source
